discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Upper level low well offshore will move move southeast and weaken today and tonight. The low will move inland over Oregon Thursday. Front associated with the low moving into Southwest Washington later today and tonight. The front will dissipate late tonight. Upper level ridge building offshore Thursday afternoon will move over Western Washington Thursday night and Friday. Another upper level low will develop off the Oregon coast over the weekend. That low will dissipate Monday. An organized front will reach the area Tuesday.
hydrology: No river flooding expected in the next 7 days.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Upper level low well offshore will move move southeast and weaken today and tonight. The low will move inland over Oregon Thursday. Front associated with the low moving into Southwest Washington later today and tonight. The front will dissipate late tonight. Upper level ridge building offshore Thursday afternoon will move over Western Washington Thursday night and Friday. Another upper level low will develop off the Oregon coast over the weekend. That low will dissipate Monday. An organized front will reach the area Tuesday.

sections.title: Short term (today through Friday)
paragraphs: Satellite imagery shows vertically stacked low near 44N/135W early this morning. Elongated front spinning out of the low well south of the area. High clouds out ahead of the front up to the Seattle area at 2 AM/10Z. Temperatures were in the 30s and lower 40s.

Upper level low moving southeast today ending up off the Central Oregon coast late this afternoon. Low level offshore flow with the cross cascade gradient bottoming out around -8 mb this morning. This will produce some breezy easterly winds in the foothills into the afternoon hours. Weakening front associated with the low moving into Southwest Washington late in the day. Reports of light rain as far north as Salem and Tillamook with ceilings in the 7000 to 9000 foot range early this morning. These conditions will make their way into Western Washington with the light rain chances as far north as around Everett by late afternoon. Any rain that does reach the surface will be light, just a few hundredths. With the cloudy skies highs will be pretty uniform, near 50.

Low not moving much tonight with what is left of the front dissipating over the southern portion of the area. Chance for light rain from about Everett southward in the evening hours. Lows in the lower 30s to lower 40s.

Weak upper level low remaining over Western Oregon Thursday. Like we saw Monday night into early Tuesday with the upper level low in the vicinity you can't totally rule out showers but most of the area will be dry Thursday. Cloud cover thinning out enough overnight for areas of fog to develop over the Southwest Interior and local river valleys in the morning. The fog will be gone by afternoon. Highs again near 50.

Upper level ridge building offshore Thursday afternoon will move over Western Washington Thursday night into Friday. Dry north northeasterly flow aloft over the area will clear skies out. Another round of morning fog Friday. With the clear skies freezing fog developing over the Southwest Interior early Friday morning. Fog dissipating by afternoon. Under sunny skies highs again near 50. Lows Friday morning in the upper 20s and 30s. Felton

sections.title: Long term (Friday night through Tuesday)
paragraphs: Extended models in a little bit better agreement this morning with the upper level ridge getting pinched off over the area Friday night and another upper level low stalling off the Oregon coast for the weekend. Bands of moisture spinning around the upper level low moving towards Western Washington. The placement of where the low stalls will be crucial to the weekend forecast. Right now a majority of the ensembles keep the low west of 130W. This will mean just glancing blows for Western Washington from the moisture bands spinning around the low. If the low ends up inside 130W much better chance for showers over the weekend. Models also in good agreement that the low dissipates Monday and an organized, but negatively tilted front, arrives Tuesday. For the most part staying with chance pops for the Saturday through Monday period with likely or higher pops Tuesday with the front.

Snow levels around 2500 feet over the weekend so snow on all the passes if the Cascades get any precipitation. Snow levels rising to 3000 to 4000 feet Monday night and Tuesday. The orientation of the front Tuesday will produce easterly winds in the passes which could trap some cool air near the surface in the passes even though the snow level might be above the pass level.
Highs in the mid 40s to lower 50s with lows in the 30s through the period. Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Terminals VFR this morning as a low pressure system spins offshore, streaming high clouds overhead. Calm winds across the southern interior has allowed patchy fog/freezing fog to develop. Expecting widespread VFR conditions later this morning. Low clouds will start to move in later this afternoon, bringing the chance for high-end MVFR/low-end VFR to some of the terminals. High-resolutation guidance suggests a 50-60% for ceilings below 3000 feet from BFI southwards. Ceilings will gradually improve this evening. Rain will start moving in along the coast after 11Z from the south and fill into the interior terminals throughout the day, with most of the rain activity focused south of BLI. Reduced visibility to 4SM possible in rain. NE winds generally 6-8 kt. Locally enhanced easterly winds through the Cascade gaps, Strait of Juan de Fuca, and near HQM with gusts 20-25 kt, decreasing into the afternoon hours.

KSEA...VFR this morning. Cloud cover will continue to fill in this morning over the terminal. There remains a chance for low-end VFR and high-end MVFR at the terminal between 00Z-06Z. High-res guidance highlights a 55% chance for ceilings below 3000 feet. NE winds 7-9 kt today will ease late tonight to 5-6 kt.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system spinning offshore continues to bring elevated seas and winds to the coastal waters. A Gale Warning remains in effect for the outer coastal waters and Small Craft Advisory for the inner coastal waters and West and Central Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas will build this morning to 10-14 feet, then decrease below 10 feet on Thursday. Grays Harbor Bar is now included in a Small Craft Advisory as seas look to build just above 10 feet. As the low pressure system continues its southeasterly trajectory into Oregon, weak high pressure will build over area waters on Thursday and Friday for benign marine conditions. Seas will decrease below 10 feet and winds will remain below advisory criteria.

The pattern will become more active starting this weekend and will continue into next week. A low pressure system offshore dropping from the Gulf of Alaska and clip area waters this weekend, which will bring elevated seas and winds. At this time, latest guidance suggests there is a 70% chance or higher for small craft advisory winds over the coastal waters and a 50-60% through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas expected to build 10-13 feet. A stronger system is set to impact the waters Monday and Tuesday. NBM guidance suggests a 70% or higher for gale winds across the coastal waters and a moderate (50-65% chance) of gales through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Additionally, guidance is also hinting a 25-35% chance for storm force gusts across the coastal waters. Seas look to build 12- 16 feet.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active and progressive pattern continues through the next week with chances for rain tonight into Wednesday and from late Friday through this weekend. Dry weather late in the workweek may be accompanied by areas of morning fog.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active and progressive pattern continues through the next week with chances for rain tonight into Wednesday and from late Friday through this weekend. Dry weather late in the workweek may be accompanied by areas of morning fog.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Transient shortwave ridging aloft remains overhead early this afternoon, while an upper low and associated surface frontal system centered well offshore of the Oregon coast will bring widespread chances for precipitation from late this evening into Wednesday. An initial warm front will lift northward, spreading a band of rain to the northeast beginning in Lincoln and Lane Counties by 8-11 PM this evening, and reaching the Columbia River by 1-3 AM Wednesday. A cold front will quickly follow on its heels, yielding another narrow band of rain overnight. Behind that boundary, steady rain will transition to hit-or-miss rain showers which persist through much of Wednesday.

Snow levels of 2500-3500 ft will allow for light accumulations in the Cascades. Chances for 1" of snow from 10 PM this evening through 10 PM Wednesday are 50-80% at the Cascade Passes, higher to the south, but chances for 3" during the same period are only 10-15%. Within the Coast Range, snow is unlikely, only a 10-25% chances for a trace of snow atop the highest peaks. An area of locally lower forecast confidence is within the Hood River Valley, where east winds will bring cooler and drier air which could support light snow or a rain/snow mix. At higher elevations near Dee and Parkdale, a period of light snow appears more likely, with 30-50% chances for accumulating snow of 0.1" or more. At lower elevations from Hood River proper to Odell, the chances for accumulating snow are lower, 10% or less, but short-range ensembles highlight a 20% chance for sufficient diabatic cooling to support at least brief periods of rain/snow mix Wednesday morning. More likely, lower elevation portions of the valley will just see a cold rain.

As the surface low nears the coast, an offshore pressure gradient will also drive east winds across the Cascades, peaking tonight into Wednesday morning. With a maximum pressure gradient of near -4 mb, peak gusts should be expected to reach 30-40 mph in the western Columbia Gorge and far eastern Portland/Vancouver metro, and slightly higher in typical locales favored for gap winds in higher terrain around the Gorge.

Behind this system, there is strong consensus for a period of dry weather from Wednesday night through much of Friday as a narrow upper-level ridge develops along the West Coast. Light winds and lingering surface moisture could allow for the development of radiation fog within sheltered valleys for the Thursday and Friday morning commutes.

Forecast uncertainty increases from late Friday through this weekend as another trough or closed low is favored to approach the coast from the Gulf of Alaska. At this lead time, the majority of long-range ensembles favor the low to be located off the north or central Oregon coast, causing the heaviest rain to occur south of Cape Blanco, while about 35% of members instead depict a scenario with the precipitation maximum occurs farther north in Oregon. In the more likely case where the surface low is located off the north/central Oregon coast, coastal winds may instead be the greatest risk, although there is a less than 10% chance wind gusts exceed 50 mph. -36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Thursday...High clouds remain in place across the area as of 0530Z Wednesday with VFR conditions. A frontal boundary continues lifting northward into northwest OR towards southwest WA, bringing rain with it. Rain has already begun at KONP, and will begin at the remaining TAF sites between 06-12Z Wednesday as a band of light rain lifts northward with the front. Chances for MVFR ceilings increase to 40-70% tonight as rain begins. Conditions will trend towards a mix of MVFR/VFR Wednesday afternoon with rain diminishing.
Gusty easterly winds are expected to develop at KPDX and KTTD tonight, with gusts up to approximately 20 kt at KPDX and 25 kt at KTTD.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions will give way to rain, gusty easterly winds, and lowering ceilings late tonight into Wednesday morning as a frontal system moves in from the south. Chances for ceilings below 3500 ft peak at 65% between 17-19Z Wednesday. -23

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Current observations as of 1 PM Tuesday afternoon show winds slowly building in the outer waters beyond 30 NM as southerly winds are expected to increase with gusts up to 40 kt. Therefore, will maintain the current suite of hazards that include a Gale Warning for zones PZZ271, PZZ272 and PZZ273 along with a Small Craft Advisory for zones PZZ251, PZZ252, PZZ253 and PZZ210.

Winds weaken Wednesday, but with seas remaining elevated around 12-16 ft at 14 seconds due to a fresh westerly swell. Thus the Gale Warning will be replaced with a Hazardous Seas Warning early Wednesday morning through at least Wednesday night. Small Craft Conditions are expected to persist for the inner waters and Columbia River Bar through at least Wednesday night as well.

Calmer conditions arrive on Thursday with seas finally falling below 10 ft and relatively light offshore winds. However, conditions look to ramp up once again for the weekend as yet another system moves towards the coast, bringing southerly winds with gusts up to 40 kt and seas building towards 14-16 ft. /42
